title: Autovacuum: what it does, when it falls behind and how to notice

videos.script: Every UPDATE in PostgreSQL leaves something behind. {{version}} The row you changed is not overwritten. A new version is written somewhere else, and the old one stays where it was, because another transaction may still be reading it. {{dead}} Once nobody can see the old version any more, it is dead. It still takes space, and nothing reuses that space until a vacuum has been through the page. {{vacuum}} Autovacuum does that for you. It wakes up once a minute, counts what each table has lost, and vacuums the tables past a threshold. {{threshold}} Most days you never think about it. This lesson is about the days you have to. {{held}} One session that opens a transaction and walks away is enough to stop it. Autovacuum runs, finishes, and removes nothing, because that one session might still read the old versions. {{counter}} Underneath all of it is a counter that cannot be allowed to run out: the transaction id. Freezing old rows is how vacuum keeps it from wrapping round, and you will watch a server refuse to work when it gets too close. {{notice}} By the end you will know which numbers to watch, and how to make the server tell you what autovacuum did. {{title}}
